CausalChain: Chronic liver injury → Activation of hepatic stellate cells → Increased TGF‐β secretion → Development of fibrosis and immunosuppression (inhibition of CD8+ T cell activity) → Impaired response to immunotherapy → CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of TGF‐β receptor in stellate cells → Reduction in TGF‐β signaling → Decreased fibrosis and restoration of immune effector function → Enhanced sensitivity of HCC to checkpoint inhibitor therapy.
Hypothesis: Selective CRISPR/Cas9 disruption of TGF‐β signaling in hepatic stellate cells will reduce fibrosis and immunosuppression in the HCC microenvironment, thereby significantly enhancing the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitor therapies in treating hepatocellular carcinoma.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is often characterized by a chronically inflamed, fibrotic, and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, largely attributed to the activation of hepatic stellate cells and the consequent production of transforming growth factor‐β (TGF‐β). Emerging gene editing techniques such as CRISPR/Cas9 offer opportunities to interfere with key signaling pathways that underpin this hostile microenvironment. We propose a therapeutic strategy in which CRISPR/Cas9 is employed to selectively knock out TGF‐β receptor expression in hepatic stellate cells in order to dampen TGF‐β mediated fibrosis and immunosuppression. In turn, this strategy is envisaged to improve the functionality of immunotherapeutic agents, particularly immune checkpoint inhibitors, thereby enhancing anti-tumor immune responses in HCC. This concept bridges genome editing with immune-based therapies, paving the way for combinatorial approaches that target both tumor cells and their supportive microenvironment.
